_comment: KRYteria's curated behavioural-indicator knowledge base.
HOW TO READ verification_status, because it is the point of this file:
pending  — drafted but NOT yet checked against a primary source. The agent CANNOT
cite it. store.list_research_notes() filters these out by default and
link_evidence() rejects a research_ref that does not resolve to a
verified row. A pending entry is invisible to the product.
verified — a human opened the source, confirmed the finding is characterised
fairly, and recorded the URL and the date.
Every entry below is PENDING. Nothing here reaches a user until somebody checks it.
WHY THE CITATIONS ARE COARSE. They name a concept, the researchers associated with
it, and a work that certainly exists — not a year, journal, volume and page I would
be reconstructing from memory. A web search on 2026-11-08 for two of the most famous
findings here (Gottman's Four Horsemen, Rusbult's Investment Model) could not settle
which primary paper to cite, and secondary sources contradicted each other on the
sample and the date. A confidently wrong bibliographic detail is exactly the failure
this whole layer exists to prevent, so the drafts stop where the confidence stops.
WHAT A GOOD ENTRY DOES. It suggests what might be worth NOTICING. It never defines a
good partner, never settles a criterion, and never licenses a label. `caveat` is not
decoration: it states what this finding cannot tell you about one person, and the
agent is required to carry it.
`do_not` is the specific misuse this particular finding invites. Those are the
sentences a model would otherwise generate.
universal_caveats: A research finding describes a tendency across many people. It does not predict one person.
Behaviour observed a handful of times is not a trait.
A finding may suggest what is worth noticing. It never settles whether a criterion is met.
Nothing here licenses naming a person's type, style, disorder, or character.

notes.finding: Gottman's conflict research identifies four communication patterns associated with relationship distress: criticism (attacking character rather than naming a behaviour), contempt (speaking from a position of superiority — mockery, sneering, name-calling), defensiveness (counter-attacking or playing the victim rather than taking any part of the point), and stonewalling (withdrawing from the interaction and stopping responding).
notes.citation: Gottman, J. M. (1994). Why Marriages Succeed or Fail: What You Can Learn from the Breakthrough Research to Make Your Marriage Last. New York: Simon & Schuster. ISBN 0-671-86748-2.
indicator_hints: Names a specific behaviour rather than generalising about who you are
Can hear a complaint without immediately counter-attacking
Stays in the conversation rather than going silent and leaving it unresolved
notes.caveat: These describe patterns across many couples, observed over time. One sharp evening is not a horseman. Gottman's predictive claims are also widely cited at precision levels the underlying studies may not support — treat this as a lens for noticing, never as a forecast.
do_not: Never tell a user their partner 'shows contempt' as an established fact from one entry.
Never quote a divorce-prediction percentage. The popular figures do not trace cleanly to primary sources.
notes.citation_checked_against: Open Library edition OL1424938M, a MARC-derived catalogue record: Simon & Schuster, New York, 1994, 234 p., ISBN-10 0671867482 / ISBN-13 9780671867485, LCCN 93035891, OCLC 28962710 and 34081834, LC call number HQ536 .G68 1994. TWO CORRECTIONS the record forced on the earlier draft. (1) The subtitle. The draft used 'And How You Can Make Yours Last', which belongs to a later edition; the 1994 Simon & Schuster edition reads 'what you can learn from the breakthrough research to make your marriage last'. (2) The authorship. The draft credited 'Gottman, J. M., & Silver, N.'; this record names John Mordechai Gottman alone, so Silver has been dropped. STILL NOT ESTABLISHED: which primary paper first defined the Four Horsemen. Sources variously credit Gottman & Buehlman (1992) or Carrere & Gottman (1999) and disagree on the samples, so the book remains the attribution. DO NOT cite a divorce-prediction percentage: the widely-quoted 94% traces only to lifestyle blogs.

notes.finding: Gottman's work describes 'repair attempts' — a joke, a softened tone, an apology, a step back mid-argument — and observes that whether a couple makes and accepts them tracks with how conflict resolves, somewhat independently of how heated the conflict gets.
notes.citation: Gottman, J. M., & Silver, N. (1999). The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work. New York: Crown Publishers.
indicator_hints: Can step back mid-argument and change the temperature
Accepts a repair attempt rather than pressing the advantage
Comes back to a conversation after cooling off
notes.caveat: Whether something was a repair attempt is a judgement, and the user is better placed to make it than a model reading a paragraph. Someone may also make repair attempts and still not meet the user's standard.
do_not: Never score a person on how often they repair.
Never treat an apology as settling a criterion — the charter names apologies as something that must not be read as evidence that earlier behaviour was harmless.
notes.citation_checked_against: A library record gives 'New York : Crown Publishers, c1999' for the first edition. A revised edition was published by Harmony in 2015 — cite whichever edition was actually read.

notes.concept: Bids for connection and turning toward
notes.finding: Gottman describes small 'bids' for attention or connection, and the response as turning toward, turning away, or turning against. The pattern of ordinary small responses is argued to matter more cumulatively than conduct during big conversations.
notes.citation: Gottman, J. M., & DeClaire, J. (2001). The Relationship Cure: A Five-Step Guide for Building Better Connections with Family, Friends, and Lovers. New York: Crown Publishers. ISBN 978-0-609-60809-8.
indicator_hints: Responds to small things you mention, not just the important ones
Notices when something is off without being told
Follows up unprompted on something you said earlier
notes.caveat: Useful precisely because it points at the ordinary and unremarkable — which is also what a journal entry is least likely to record. Absence of bid-related evidence means the journal did not capture it, not that it did not happen.
do_not: Never infer that someone 'turns away' from an entry that simply did not mention small moments.
notes.citation_checked_against: The 2001 Crown hardcover (ISBN 9780609608098) is the first edition. The commonly-seen subtitle 'A 5 Step Guide to Strengthening Your Marriage, Family, and Friendships' belongs to the later paperback (ISBN 9780609809532) — the drafted citation previously used the wrong subtitle.

notes.finding: Gottman's research describes 'flooding' — a state of physiological arousal during conflict in which people become much less able to take in new information or de-escalate, and often withdraw. It offers a non-character explanation for why someone shuts down mid-argument.
notes.citation: Gottman, J. M., & Silver, N. (1999). The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work. New York: Crown Publishers.
indicator_hints: Can say they need a break rather than simply disappearing
Comes back after taking time, rather than leaving it unresolved
Takes time without using the silence as a punishment
notes.caveat: This is a mechanism, not an excuse. Needing a break and using silence as leverage look similar from outside and are different things; only the user can tell which they experienced.
do_not: Never offer flooding as a reason the user should not be bothered by withdrawal.
Never diagnose anyone as flooded. It is a physiological state nobody can see from a journal entry.
notes.citation_checked_against: Same work as gottman-repair-attempts; first edition Crown, 1999, revised edition Harmony, 2015.

notes.finding: Attachment research, extended from Bowlby and Ainsworth's work on children to adult romantic relationships by Hazan and Shaver and others, describes individual differences in how people seek and respond to closeness — broadly, more secure, more anxious, and more avoidant tendencies.
notes.attribution: John Bowlby; Mary Ainsworth; Cindy Hazan and Phillip Shaver
notes.citation: Hazan, C., & Shaver, P. R. (1987). Romantic love conceptualized as an attachment process. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 52(3), 511–524. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.52.3.511
notes.citation_checked_against: PubMed record 3572722 (1987 Mar;52(3):511-24), corroborated by a Springer reference list giving the same volume, pages and DOI.
indicator_hints: Can say what they need directly rather than testing whether you notice
Closeness after a disagreement is restored rather than withheld
Does not treat a request for space, or for reassurance, as an accusation
notes.caveat: THE HIGHEST-RISK ENTRY IN THIS FILE. Attachment language is the most over-applied vocabulary in popular relationship writing, and the charter names it explicitly: attachment theory must not let the agent diagnose somebody's attachment style from three text messages. Tendencies are measured with instruments, over time, with the person's participation — none of which a journal provides.
do_not: NEVER assign an attachment style to anybody, in any wording, however hedged.
Never say 'this sounds like anxious attachment' or 'that is avoidant behaviour'.
Never use attachment language about the user either.
Use this only to suggest behaviours worth noticing — never as an explanation of who somebody is.

notes.finding: Gross's process model distinguishes strategies for handling emotion — among them reappraisal (changing how a situation is construed) and suppression (inhibiting the outward expression of a feeling already present). The two are associated with different outcomes, and suppression tends to carry more interpersonal cost.
notes.citation: Gross, J. J. (Ed.). (2014). Handbook of Emotion Regulation (2nd ed.). New York: Guilford Press.
indicator_hints: Can name what they are feeling rather than acting it out sideways
Does not make the other person responsible for managing their feeling
Can be upset and still be fair in the same conversation
notes.caveat: Someone appearing calm may be regulating well or suppressing heavily, and those look identical from outside. Do not read composure as maturity.
do_not: Never treat visible calm as evidence a criterion about emotional maturity is met.
notes.citation_checked_against: PARTIAL. Gross as editor and Guilford as publisher are confirmed across editions; the 2nd edition (2014) is confirmed. The FIRST edition's 2007 date is NOT confirmed — one listing gives 08/2009. A 3rd edition (Gross & Ford, 2024) now exists. Cite the edition actually read.

notes.finding: Rusbult's Investment Model proposes that commitment is shaped by three factors that vary independently: satisfaction with the relationship, the perceived quality of alternatives, and the size of what has already been invested. It accounts for why commitment and satisfaction can come apart — someone may stay while unhappy because investment is high or perceived alternatives are poor.
notes.citation: Rusbult, C. E. (1980). Commitment and satisfaction in romantic associations: A test of the investment model. Journal of Experimental Social Psychology, 16(2), 172–186. https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-1031(80)90007-4
indicator_hints: What you say you want, set against what you are choosing to do
Reasons for staying that are about what has already been spent rather than about the relationship now
notes.caveat: This is the entry most relevant to KRYteria's own thesis, and therefore the one most likely to be over-applied. It is a framework for the USER to examine their own reasoning with — never a reason to tell somebody they are staying for the wrong reasons.
do_not: Never tell a user they are only staying because of sunk cost.
Never use this to argue toward leaving. The charter is explicit: no automatic stay/leave recommendations.
notes.citation_checked_against: A Northwestern-hosted PDF reproduces the journal header ('JOURNAL OF EXPERIMENTAL SOCIAL PSYCHOLOGY 16, 172-186 (1980)'); Scilit gives the same volume, issue and pages. An earlier search on 2026-11-07 could NOT settle this; a targeted search did.

notes.finding: Reis and Shaver's intimacy process model describes intimacy as built through a cycle of disclosure and response, where what matters is the discloser's perception that they were understood, validated, and cared for. Perceived responsiveness, rather than disclosure alone, is the active ingredient.
notes.citation: Reis, H. T., & Shaver, P. (1988). Intimacy as an interpersonal process. In S. W. Duck (Ed.), Handbook of Personal Relationships. Chichester: Wiley.
indicator_hints: You feel understood rather than merely heard out
Remembers what matters to you without prompting
Responds to the thing you actually said
notes.caveat: Responsiveness is defined by the discloser's experience. That makes the user the authority here, and the model emphatically not.
do_not: Never tell a user whether their partner was responsive. Ask them.
notes.citation_checked_against: STILL PENDING, but further along than it was. The CONTAINER is now confirmed against a qualifying source: Open Library edition OL2392678M is Duck, S. (ed.), 'Handbook of personal relationships: theory, research, and interventions', Wiley, Chichester [England] and New York, 1988, 702 p., ISBN-10 0471914916, LCCN 87022168, OCLC 16527128. That settles editor, book, publisher, place and year. WHAT IS STILL MISSING: that the Reis & Shaver chapter sits in THIS volume, and at what pages. The Open Library record carries no table of contents, and the Library of Congress catalogue, whose MARC record would carry a 505 contents note, is not reachable from this machine (both lccn.loc.gov/87022168 and its marcxml endpoint time out). This entry needs a catalogue record or publisher table of contents listing the chapter. AND THE EARLIER SOURCE WAS WRONG. The URL once recorded here was PubMed 9599440, which is Laurenceau, Barrett & Pietromonaco (1998), JPSP 74(5), 1238-1251 -- a different work that shares the title. Do not confuse them.

notes.finding: Gable and colleagues studied how people respond to a partner's good news, distinguishing active-constructive responses (engaged, enthusiastic) from passive or destructive ones. How good news is received is associated with relationship wellbeing, in some work more strongly than how bad news is handled.
notes.citation: Gable, S. L., Reis, H. T., Impett, E. A., & Asher, E. R. (2004). What do you do when things go right? The intrapersonal and interpersonal benefits of sharing positive events. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 87(2), 228–245. https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.87.2.228
notes.citation_checked_against: PubMed record 15301629, corroborated by the author-hosted PDF at Rochester reproducing the journal header. One coaching site lists a different title, 'Capitalizing on Daily Positive Events' — that appears to be an error.
indicator_hints: Is visibly pleased when something goes well for you
Asks about the good thing rather than changing the subject
Does not compete with or deflate your news
notes.caveat: A useful counterweight: most relationship journalling records problems, so a criterion assessed only from conflict entries is assessed from half the evidence. Worth suggesting the user notice, not worth inferring from absence.
do_not: Never read the absence of good-news entries as evidence of poor responses.

notes.finding: Overall and colleagues' work on how partners attempt change distinguishes direct strategies (stating the problem and the request openly) from indirect ones (hinting, withdrawing, sulking). Direct approaches can feel worse in the moment while being associated with more actual change over time.
notes.citation: Overall, N. C., Fletcher, G. J. O., Simpson, J. A., & Sibley, C. G. (2009). Regulating partners in intimate relationships: The costs and benefits of different communication strategies. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 96(3).
indicator_hints: Says what they want rather than expecting it to be inferred
A raised concern is engaged with rather than waited out
Change that was agreed to actually happens
notes.caveat: Directness is not universally safe or available. Where a safety concern exists, encouraging a user to be more direct may be actively dangerous — the charter prohibits encouraging confrontation where safety may be at risk.
do_not: Never suggest a user be more direct when the safety layer has fired.
Never frame a user's indirectness as their failing.
notes.citation_checked_against: PARTIAL. A University of Minnesota listing confirms volume 96, issue 3, March 2009, and the full title (note the subtitle, which the draft omitted). THE PAGE RANGE IS NOT CONFIRMED — it is commonly given as 620–639, but no source in the search stated it. Find the pages before citing them.

notes.finding: Baumeister and Leary argued that the need for frequent, stable, caring connection is a fundamental human motivation, and that much social behaviour is better explained by it than by preference.
notes.citation: Baumeister, R. F., & Leary, M. R. (1995). The need to belong: Desire for interpersonal attachments as a fundamental human motivation. Psychological Bulletin, 117(3), 497–529. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-2909.117.3.497
notes.citation_checked_against: PubMed record 7777651 (1995 May;117(3):497-529), corroborated by the Duke Scholars listing.
notes.caveat: Context rather than an indicator. Useful as a reason not to treat somebody's reluctance to end a relationship as weakness — the pull toward connection is not a character flaw. No behavioural indicator should be generated from this.
do_not: Never generate a checklist item from this.
Never use it to explain a user's choices back to them.

notes.finding: Gouldner described reciprocity as a near-universal social norm: a benefit received generates an obligation to return one. The obligation operates whether or not the benefit was wanted.
notes.citation: Gouldner, A. W. (1960). The norm of reciprocity: A preliminary statement. American Sociological Review, 25(2), 161–178. https://doi.org/10.2307/2092623
indicator_hints: Generosity that carries no expectation attached to it
A gift or favour is not referred back to later as leverage
notes.caveat: Directly relevant to KRYteria's worked example about paying for dinner. Reciprocity explains why a gesture creates a feeling of obligation — which is a reason to be MORE careful about reading generosity as evidence of care, not less.
do_not: Never map a gift, a payment, or a favour as supporting a criterion about care or character on its own.
notes.citation_checked_against: Multiple citation databases agree on 25(2), 161–178, April 1960, DOI 10.2307/2092623. One Scinapse record shows '161-161', which looks like a truncated entry rather than a conflict.

notes.finding: People systematically over-attribute others' behaviour to stable character and under-weight situational causes, while explaining their own behaviour the opposite way. The asymmetry is one of the most replicated findings in social psychology.
notes.attribution: Lee Ross; Edward Jones and Victor Harris
notes.citation: Ross, L. (1977). The intuitive psychologist and his shortcomings: Distortions in the attribution process. In L. Berkowitz (Ed.), Advances in Experimental Social Psychology (Vol. 10, pp. 173–220). New York: Academic Press.
notes.caveat: This one governs the agent's own behaviour more than the user's. It is the research basis for the charter's rule against treating an isolated event as a personality trait — including when the model is the one doing it.
do_not: Never generate a checklist item from this.
Use it as a check on the agent's own output: a finding that explains behaviour by character, with a situational reading unconsidered, is probably this error.
notes.citation_checked_against: Settled from the DOI's own registered metadata, retrieved by content negotiation against doi.org (Accept: application/x-bibtex) rather than from a page about the work. The registration returns: author Lee Ross; title 'The Intuitive Psychologist And His Shortcomings: Distortions in the Attribution Process'; booktitle 'Advances in Experimental Social Psychology Volume 10'; year 1977; pages 173-220; ISBN 9780120152100; ISSN 0065-2601. That confirms the page range, which had previously rested on a single citation guide, and confirms the DOI itself, which had been inferred from a PII on a third-party page. The publisher's own page (ScienceDirect) returns HTTP 403 to automated fetching, which is why the registry was used instead. ONE DIFFERENCE, not an error: the registration names the publisher as Elsevier, its present owner. The citation keeps 'New York: Academic Press', the imprint that actually published the 1977 volume.

notes.finding: People preferentially seek, notice, and recall information consistent with what they already believe, and weigh disconfirming evidence less. The effect operates without awareness and is not reduced by caring about accuracy.
notes.citation: Nickerson, R. S. (1998). Confirmation bias: A ubiquitous phenomenon in many guises. Review of General Psychology, 2(2), 175–220.
notes.citation_checked_against: The UCSD-hosted PDF reproduces the journal header (1998, Vol. 2, No. 2, 175-220); Scinapse and CiNii give the same volume, issue and pages.
notes.caveat: The research basis for storing counter-evidence as a first-class row rather than a footnote, and for interrogating favourable conclusions as hard as unfavourable ones. It applies to the agent exactly as much as to the user.
do_not: Never tell a user they are exhibiting confirmation bias. Show them the counter-evidence and let them look at it.

notes.finding: Stark's work reframes much intimate-partner abuse as a pattern of control over a person's autonomy — monitoring, isolation from support, restriction of money and movement, and rule-setting — rather than as discrete violent incidents. The pattern can be present with little or no physical violence.
notes.citation: Stark, E. (2007). Coercive Control: How Men Entrap Women in Personal Life. New York: Oxford University Press. ISBN 978-0-19-515427-6.
notes.caveat: SAFETY-ADJACENT AND TIGHTLY BOUNDED. This may inform the language the safety layer uses to describe a behaviour — 'that behaviour may be a form of coercive control' — and nothing else. It must never be used to classify a person, to assess a criterion, or to tell a user what their situation is. The charter is explicit that recognising a behaviour and labelling an individual are different acts.
do_not: NEVER conclude that a relationship is coercively controlling.
NEVER say a person is an abuser, in any wording.
Never generate a checklist item from this. Nobody should be ticking boxes about whether they are being abused.
Never use it to pressure a user toward leaving or reporting.
notes.citation_checked_against: Library and bookseller records agree on Oxford University Press, 2007, hardback ISBN 978-0-19-515427-6, Interpersonal Violence series. Page counts differ (452 vs 464) and one catalogue inverts the title and subtitle; neither affects the citation.

notes.finding: Johnson's work on emotionally focused therapy describes 'attachment injuries' — moments of abandonment or betrayal at a point of need that remain live and resurface in later conflict until addressed directly.
notes.citation: Johnson, S. (2008). Hold Me Tight: Seven Conversations for a Lifetime of Love (1st ed.). New York: Little, Brown. ISBN 978-0-316-11300-7.
indicator_hints: A hurt that was raised is acknowledged rather than argued down
The same unresolved moment stops resurfacing after it is addressed
notes.caveat: Drawn from a clinical framework. KRYteria is explicitly not therapy, and this must inform noticing only — never anything resembling a treatment suggestion.
do_not: Never suggest a therapeutic intervention or exercise.
Never tell a user they have an attachment injury.
notes.citation_checked_against: Daystar University library catalogue record 0000047085: 'Hold me tight : seven conversations for a lifetime of love /', main author 'Johnson, Sue, 1947-', Little, Brown & Co., New York, 2008, 1st ed., LC call number HQ801 .J64 2008. This replaces the publisher and retailer listings the draft rested on, which were all commercial. The '(1st ed.)' in the citation comes from this record. ISBN: the record does not print one in its bibliographic fields; 031611300X appears in its cover-image link, and that ISBN-10 is the same book as the ISBN-13 978-0-316-11300-7 in the citation. A Michigan State catalogue record was tried first and returned HTTP 404. NOTE ON THE SOURCE: a .ac.ke record qualifies under backend/sources.py only because the academic-TLD rule was generalised on 2026-11-11 from an enumerated list to the .ac.<cc> / .edu.<cc> pattern. That was a deliberate widening, recorded in the rules file, not a workaround for this entry.

notes.finding: Arkes and Blumer showed people continue investing in a course of action because of what has already been spent, even when future prospects alone would not justify it. The effect is robust and operates in time and effort as well as money.
notes.citation: Arkes, H. R., & Blumer, C. (1985). The psychology of sunk cost. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 35(1), 124–140. https://doi.org/10.1016/0749-5978(85)90049-4
notes.caveat: Pairs with the Investment Model and carries the same risk. A long investment is a legitimate reason to want something to work; it is not automatically an error. Offer it as a question the user can ask themselves, never as a diagnosis of their reasoning.
do_not: Never tell a user they are falling for sunk cost.
Never generate a checklist item from this.
notes.citation_checked_against: The journal header reads 'ORGANIZATIONAL BEHAVIOR AND HUMAN DECISION PROCESSES 35, 124-140 (1985)'; a bibliographic record gives the same volume, pages and DOI. Source URL is the DOI rather than a university's copy of the PDF.

notes.finding: Behaviour reinforced unpredictably is more persistent than behaviour reinforced consistently. The finding is foundational in learning research and well replicated across species and settings.
notes.attribution: B. F. Skinner and the operant conditioning literature
notes.citation: Ferster, C. B., & Skinner, B. F. (1957). Schedules of Reinforcement. New York: Appleton-Century-Crofts.
notes.caveat: HIGH MISUSE RISK. This is popularly deployed to tell people their inconsistent partner is conditioning them, which is both unfalsifiable from a journal and insulting. It may inform why an inconsistent pattern is worth noticing. It may not explain a user's feelings back to them.
do_not: Never tell a user they are being intermittently reinforced.
Never attribute intent to an inconsistent pattern.
Never generate a checklist item from this.
notes.citation_checked_against: Library catalogue records agree: New York, Appleton-Century-Crofts, 1957, 741 pages, Century Psychology Series, LCCN 57006418. One Goodreads edition lists Prentice-Hall, which appears to be a catalogue error.

notes.finding: What people say they value and what their choices reveal frequently diverge. The gap is well documented across economics and psychology and is not generally explained by dishonesty.
notes.attribution: Paul Samuelson (revealed preference); subsequent behavioural literature
notes.citation: Samuelson, P. A. (1938). A note on the pure theory of consumer's behaviour. Economica (New Series), 5(17), 61–71. https://doi.org/10.2307/2548836
notes.caveat: KRYteria's founding premise, so it needs the most careful handling. The gap is ordinary and human, not a failing. The product exists to make it visible to the user — never to point it out as a verdict about them.
do_not: Never tell a user their actions reveal they do not really want what they said.
Show the record and let them draw it.
notes.citation_checked_against: Several sources agree on 5(17), February 1938, 61–71, DOI 10.2307/2548836, JSTOR 2548836. Note the fuller treatment is the 1948 Economica paper 'Consumption Theory in Terms of Revealed Preference', 15(60), 243–253 — cite the 1938 paper only for the original framing.
